# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: p3-disc-setup
#| include: false

loadNamespace("mlogit")
n_coef_2b <- length(stats::coef(model_2b_exploded_draw_final))

pct_diff_top <- 100 * (1 - score_agreement_3_vs_2b$share_same_top)

d1_meta   <- model_3_depth1_diag_meta
d1_cv     <- d1_meta$cv_summary$fold_mean_pl_r2
d3_cv     <- gbt_selected_config$fold_mean_pl_r2
boot_d1_plr2 <- boot_ranking_3_vs_depth1 |> dplyr::filter(metric == "test_pl_r2")

n_across_train_pos <- sum(gbt_perm_importance_across_train$mean_drop > 0)
n_across_test_neg  <- sum(gbt_perm_importance_across_test$mean_drop < 0)
```

The series has changed one thing at a time: paper 2a changed the feature
set, paper 2b changed the objective, and this paper changes the function
class. A gradient-boosted ensemble with depth-3 interactions and
`r model_3_gbt_meta$nrounds` trees ranks no better than a linear predictor
with `r n_coef_2b` terms, fitted on the identical objective, features,
split and metrics as this one: the paired bootstrap against paper 2b
(@sec-results) contains zero on P1_rank, on Brier_place, and on test
pseudo-$R^2$ alike. This is not two routes to the same model. Their
within-race-centred scores correlate at $r =$
`r sprintf("%.3f", score_agreement_3_vs_2b$pearson_r)`, and they pick a
different top horse in `r sprintf("%.0f", pct_diff_top)`% of test races —
two different models that rank equally well.

The reading is that the linear predictor was not the binding constraint.
Neither a linear combination of these features nor a tree ensemble with
real interaction depth closes any distance to the market on this
objective, so whatever limits both is not the form of the function
reading the features — it is more likely the information the features
themselves carry. That makes the feature set the natural next lever, not
the function class. It is worth stating plainly: a marginal improvement
here would have left the function-class question open for a later paper
to revisit; a clean tie closes it, and that is a more useful result than
a marginal improvement would have been.

Set against that tie, the one contrast in the paper that is
distinguishable is the market. Its discounted-Harville probabilities beat
the model decisively on both ranking metrics — P1_rank by
`r sprintf("%.2e", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$diff_point[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "P1_rank"])`
[`r sprintf("%.2e", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$ci_lo[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "P1_rank"])`,
`r sprintf("%.2e", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$ci_hi[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "P1_rank"])`],
Brier_place by
`r sprintf("%.4f", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$diff_point[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "Brier_place"])`
[`r sprintf("%.4f", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$ci_lo[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "Brier_place"])`,
`r sprintf("%.4f", boot_ranking_3_vs_market$ci_hi[boot_ranking_3_vs_market$metric == "Brier_place"])`]
— as it has beaten every model this series has tried, on the win
objective in papers 1 and 2a and on the ranking objective in paper 2b.
Three changes to the model in turn have each left that gap untouched.

Five limitations are stated here rather than left for a reader to find.

- **Tuning asymmetry.** The linear models in this series were reduced by
  a hand-run significance rule; this model was selected from a 72-point,
  cross-validated grid. That is a capacity-and-selection asymmetry, and on
  its own a live alternative explanation for any difference found. Two
  things temper it: the grid is nearly flat near its maximum — only
  `r n_within_1se` of 72 points sit within one paired standard error of
  it — and the model given the more generous search did not win.
- **Row-level subsampling.** XGBoost draws its row subsample from
  individual horses; the likelihood's own grouping unit is the race, and
  the two do not match. Dropping some of a race's runners at random
  changes the remaining runners' own gradients and Hessians, not merely
  how many rows are left. Every one of the top ten tuning configurations
  used subsampling at 0.7, so it clearly helps; the mismatch between the
  two units is unresolved.
- **Gain importance is in-sample.** It is an accounting of where the
  fitted loss went, not evidence a feature helps out of sample.
- **The Hessian is an approximation.** The custom objective supplies
  XGBoost one Hessian value per row, the diagonal of a likelihood whose
  true Hessian couples every runner still in contention within a race.
- **Going affinity measures ground-type form, not a preference for
  today's going.** AW going is `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_standard_train)`%
  Standard across the training races, so the feature reaching the model
  is mostly a horse's record on Standard-or-Good ground relative to its
  own career rate. The question paper 2b deferred to this paper has been
  answered only in the weaker sense this data permits.

A depth-3 fit's advantage over a depth-1 (stumps only, additive)
diagnostic model appears in cross-validation — fold-mean pseudo-$R^2$
`r sprintf("%.4f", d3_cv)` against `r sprintf("%.4f", d1_cv)` — and
in-sample — `r sprintf("%.4f", model_3_gbt_meta$train_pl_r2)` against
`r sprintf("%.4f", d1_meta$train_pl_r2)` — where both the folds and the
training data are drawn from the same era the model is fitted on. It is
absent on the chronologically later test split
(`r sprintf("%+.4f", boot_d1_plr2$diff_point)`, 90% CI
[`r sprintf("%.4f", boot_d1_plr2$ci_lo)`, `r sprintf("%.4f", boot_d1_plr2$ci_hi)`]).
The race-level features show the same pattern from another angle: all
five permutation drops are positive on the training split
(`r n_across_train_pos` of 5) and `r n_across_test_neg` of 5 are negative
on the test split.

We state the direction and stop there. An interval containing zero is
consistent with era-specific structure that does not carry forward to
later data, with ordinary sampling noise, and with a test set too small
to separate the two; deciding between them needs several chronological
blocks and a longer span of data than 2006–2015 provides, which we do not
have. We do not adjudicate, and this observation is not offered as the
paper's explanation for the null result above. The depth-1 fit is a
diagnostic, not a candidate: its test-split numbers were computed only
after model selection had closed, and it was never eligible to be chosen.

The series has now changed the features, the objective, and the function
class, and none has closed the gap to the market. What is left is the
information reaching the model in the first place — hand-built summaries
of a horse's run history rather than the run history itself — and
learning a representation of that history directly, on the same ranking
objective, is the direction under consideration next. Separately: the two
models disagree on the top pick in `r sprintf("%.0f", pct_diff_top)`% of
test races, which suggests a rule that backs only where they agree.
That cannot be evaluated here — the disagreement figures come from the
test split, and building and testing a rule on them would be selection on
the data meant to test it — and it carries a caution worth recording
alongside it: two independently-specified models are more likely to
agree where both are confident, which tends to mean a shorter-priced
horse, and the starting-price margin bites hardest at short prices, so a
higher strike rate on an agreement subset need not mean a better return.
Neither is a result of this paper; both are left as open directions.
